You might think using an AI chatbot for medical advice is a terrible idea, but hundreds of millions of people do it every week.

A recent lawsuit has revealed a near-fatal case: ChatGPT advised a pastor to ignore the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism, a condition with a 30% mortality rate. The advice it gave almost certainly made things worse...

AI chatbots can help you in many ways, but replacing a visit to the doctor is not one of them. Given that they frequently make up nonsense with complete confidence, they're not even a good replacement for a Google search.

Yet according to OpenAI's own records, hundreds of millions of people ask ChatGPT health questions every week. Similarly, analysis has found that health questions are among the most common query types in Microsoft's Copilot mobile app.

If you need any evidence of the potential consequences of relying on chatbots for medical advice, a lawsuit filed by a pastor in Florida provides an illuminating example. According to The New York Times, he is suing OpenAI because ChatGPT told him not to worry about his pulmonary embolism symptoms.

ChatGPT advised him to simply rest. Not only did it tell him not to seek medical attention, but remaining still for extended periods is exactly the worst thing you can do in such situations—and I say this because I once ended up with a pulmonary embolism after a twelve-hour flight with a broken leg. Researchers knew about this risk back then, but it wasn't communicated to patients.

When Winters was finally admitted to the ICU, doctors said his symptoms were most likely caused by a series of pulmonary embolisms, and the reason his condition had worsened was that he had followed ChatGPT's advice and sat still for weeks on end.

The report notes that Winters was using GPT-4o, an older ChatGPT model known for its tendency toward 'sycophantic' responses. This may explain why the reply mentioned trusting in God, but regardless of which AI model you're using, never let it make medical decisions for you.
